content: A disability is defined as a condition or functional limitation that is significantly impaired compared to the typical standard of an individual or their group. This term is commonly used to describe impairments in physical, sensory, cognitive, intellectual, or mental functioning, as well as chronic diseases. This perspective aligns with the medical model of disability, which focuses on the individual's condition. In contrast, the human rights or social model of disability emphasizes the interaction between an individual and their environment. This model highlights the role of societal factors, such as attitudes or accessibility, in labeling, causing, or perpetuating disability. It underscores how societal structures often favor the majority, potentially marginalizing individuals with disabilities. Disabilities can occur at any point in a person’s life or may be present from birth. On December 13, 2006, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, marking the first human rights treaty of the 21st century. This treaty aims to protect and promote the rights and opportunities of the estimated 650 million people with disabilities worldwide. Countries that ratify the convention are required to implement national laws and repeal outdated ones to ensure equal rights for individuals with disabilities. These rights include access to education, employment, and cultural life, the ability to own and inherit property, freedom from discrimination in marriage and family life, and protection from being unwilling subjects in medical experiments. In 1976, the United Nations declared 1981 as the International Year for Disabled Persons, later renamed the International Year of Disabled Persons. This initiative was followed by the UN Decade of Disabled Persons (1983–1993), which included the World Programme of Action Concerning Disabled Persons. During the planning of the International Year of Disabled Persons in 1981, Frank Bowe was the sole representative with a disability involved in the process. Today, many countries appoint representatives with disabilities to advocate for their communities. The decade concluded with an address to the General Assembly by Robert Davila, who, like Bowe, is deaf. In 1984, UNESCO formally recognized sign language as a valid medium for the education of deaf children and youth, marking a significant step forward in inclusive education.
